content: Bearberry refers to three species of dwarf shrubs within the genus Arctostaphylos. Unlike other species in this genus, such as Manzanita, bearberries are specifically adapted to arctic and sub-arctic climates. They exhibit a circumpolar distribution, being found in northern regions of North America, Asia, and Europe. One species has a small, highly disjunct population in Central America. The name bearberry originates from the plant's edible fruit, which is said to be highly favored by bears. The berries themselves are edible and are sometimes harvested for food. Additionally, the leaves of the plant are utilized in herbal medicine. Species 1. Alpine Bearberry (Arctostaphylos alpina) This is a low-growing shrub, typically 10–30 cm in height. Its leaves are not evergreen, but dead leaves persist on the stems for several years. The berries are dark purple to black in color. Distribution: Circumpolar, found at high latitudes from Scotland across Scandinavia, Russia, Alaska, Canada, and Greenland. Its southern limits in Europe include the Pyrenees and the Alps, while in Asia, it extends to the Altay Mountains. In North America, it is found as far south as British Columbia in the west and Maine and New Hampshire in the east. 2. Red Bearberry (Arctostaphylos rubra) This is another low-growing shrub, also 10–30 cm in height. Its leaves are deciduous, falling in autumn to leave bare stems. The berries are red. Distribution: Found in the mountains of Sichuan, southwestern China, extending north and east to eastern Siberia, Alaska, and northern Canada, reaching as far east as northern Quebec. 3. Common Bearberry (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi) This species has been known by various names, including Arberry, Bear’s Grape, Crowberry, Foxberry, Hog Cranberry, Kinnikinnick, Mealberry, Mountain Box, Mountain Cranberry, Mountain Tobacco, Red Bearberry, Sandberry, Upland Cranberry, and Uva-ursi. Medicinal Uses Bearberry contains several bioactive compounds, including arbutin, methyl arbutin, ursolic acid, tannic acid, gallic acid, hydroquinones (primarily arbutin, up to 17%), tannins (up to 15%), phenolic glycosides, flavonoids, essential oils, and resins. The leaves are harvested during the summer and dried for use in infusions, liquid extracts, medicinal tea bags, and tablets. The plant is claimed to have the following medicinal properties: Anti-lithic (prevents stone formation) Aromatic Astringent Disinfectant Diuretic Lithontriptic (dissolves stones) Renal sedative Mild stimulant Tonic Urinary antiseptic Bearberry has been used to treat a wide range of conditions, including: Arthritis Lower back pain Bedwetting Bile problems Bladder infections Bloating Bright’s disease Bronchitis Bladder catarrh Cystitis Diabetes (by reducing excessive blood sugar) Diarrhea Fevers Fluid retention Gallstones Gonorrhea Headaches (when smoked) Hemorrhoids Indigestion Kidney stones Kidney infections Liver problems Lung congestion Excessive menstruation Nephritis Obesity Pancreatitis Prostate gland weakness Rheumatism Chronic urethritis Vaginal discharge and diseases Water retention It is also claimed to strengthen the heart muscle and urinary tract, help the womb return to its normal size after childbirth, and prevent uterine infections. Additionally, it is said to act as a powerful tonic for the bladder sphincter muscle, aiding in bladder control issues. Bearberry exhibits strong bacteriostatic activity against Staphylococcus and E. coli. The leaves possess potent astringent properties. While bearberry is generally considered safe, large doses may cause adverse effects such as nausea, green urine, bluish-gray skin, vomiting, fever, chills, severe back pain, and ringing in the ears. Some individuals can tolerate up to 20 grams, while others may show signs of poisoning after consuming just 1 gram. It is recommended not to use bearberry for more than 7–10 days at a time. It should not be used by pregnant or breastfeeding individuals, children under 12, or patients with kidney disease. Drug interactions have been noted with diuretics and medications that acidify the urine (e.g., ascorbic acid and Urex). History and Folklore Bearberry was first documented in the 13th-century Welsh herbal The Physicians of Myddfai. It was later described by Clusius in 1601 and recommended for medicinal use in 1763 by Gerhard and others. The plant appeared in the London Pharmacopoeia in 1788, though it was likely in use long before this. In Strathnairn, Scotland, a hill known in Gaelic as Cnoc nan Cnàimhseag translates to The Hill of the Bearberries. Marco Polo reported in the 13th century that the Chinese used bearberry as a diuretic to treat kidney and urinary problems. Bearberry leaves are still used medicinally in Poland and other countries. Native Americans incorporated bearberry into religious ceremonies, often mixing it with tobacco and other herbs. When smoked in a sacred pipe, it was believed to carry prayers to the Great Spirit. Mixed with tobacco, it was called Kinnikinnick, derived from the Algonquian word for mixture. Native Americans also used bearberry tea to treat urinary tract inflammation, urethritis, kidney stones, and cystitis. The Cheyenne used the tea for back sprains, while other tribes powdered the leaves to apply to sores or drank it to treat venereal diseases. The berries were sometimes made into a tea to combat obesity. Early European settlers in the Americas used bearberry leaves internally as an astringent to treat nephritis, kidney stones, and other urinary system diseases.
